accuracy	Accuracy describes how close their average is to the true value. A refractometer can be precise and inaccurate at once: it gives the same reading every time, and that reading is wrong.	upstream chapter-0 term
brew ratio	Mass of brew water divided by mass of dry coffee. Chapter 2A.	upstream chapter-0 term
buffer	Mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists pH change; brewed coffee is one. Appendix A.	upstream chapter-0 term
buffer solution	A pH meter is calibrated with two buffer solutions of known pH that bracket the samples (pH 4 and 7 for coffee) and rinsed between samples.	upstream chapter-0 term
calibration	Only calibration, comparing the instrument against something whose value is known, removes systematic error.	upstream chapter-0 term
drift	Drift is a slow change of reading with time. Load cells drift as they warm, and a cup of hot coffee loses a few tenths of a gram per minute by evaporation.	upstream chapter-0 term
endpoint	In a titration, a base of known concentration (here sodium hydroxide, NaOH) is added to a measured volume of brew until the pH reaches a chosen endpoint.	upstream chapter-0 term
extraction yield	Mass of coffee solids dissolved into the brew as a fraction of the dry dose. Chapter 2A.	upstream chapter-0 term
in quadrature	The rule for combining them is called addition in quadrature: square the individual uncertainties, add the squares, and take the square root.	upstream chapter-0 term
least squares	The method of least squares chooses the slope and intercept that make the sum of squared vertical distances from the points to the line as small as possible (Appendix E.5).	upstream chapter-0 term
linearity	Linearity is whether the reading is proportional to the true mass across the range you use.	upstream chapter-0 term
load cell	Coffee and kitchen scales weigh with a load cell, a metal element whose electrical resistance changes slightly as it bends under load.	upstream chapter-0 term
measurement uncertainty	That statement is the uncertainty, written after the value with a plus-or-minus sign.	upstream chapter-0 term
particle size distribution	A grind is described by its particle size distribution, the proportion of material in each range of particle sizes.	upstream chapter-0 term
pH	pH measures the hydrogen ions that are free in solution at the moment of measurement: pH = −log<sub>10</sub>[H<sup>+</sup>], with [H<sup>+</sup>] in mol/L (Appendix A.5).	upstream chapter-0 term
precision	Precision describes how closely repeated readings agree with each other. Accuracy describes how close their average is to the true value.	upstream chapter-0 term
random error	Random error scatters repeated readings around their average. The last digit of a refractometer flickers; one pour is a gram heavier than the next.	upstream chapter-0 term
reflectance	A reflectance instrument shines light on a sample, usually ground coffee pressed flat, and measures the fraction reflected.	upstream chapter-0 term
refractive index	The amount of bending depends on the refractive index of each material, a number that rises as more material is dissolved in a liquid.	upstream chapter-0 term
refractometer	A refractometer measures the refractive index of a drop of liquid on a glass prism.	upstream chapter-0 term
repeatability	Repeatability is the standard deviation of repeated weighings of one object, removing and replacing it each time.	upstream chapter-0 term
resolution	Resolution is the smallest step the display shows. It is not the uncertainty: a scale that displays 0.1 g may repeat only to 0.2 g.	upstream chapter-0 term
response time	A probe also has a response time: a thick probe can take thirty seconds to settle.	upstream chapter-0 term
sample standard deviation	The scatter of n repeated readings x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>, …, x<sub>n</sub> is measured by the standard deviation, s, defined in Appendix E.1.	upstream chapter-0 term
significant figures	Digits that the uncertainty does not support are not significant figures.  ### Combining uncertainties	upstream chapter-0 term
standard error of the mean	Its uncertainty is the standard error:	upstream chapter-0 term
systematic error	Systematic error shifts every reading in the same direction by the same amount. A thermometer that reads 2 °C low is wrong by 2 °C every time, so averaging a hundred readings leaves the 2 °C error untouched.	upstream chapter-0 term
threshold	A threshold is the smallest concentration of a substance that the taster can detect.	upstream chapter-0 term
titratable acidity	Amount of base needed to bring a sample to a set pH endpoint (8.2 for coffee); predicts sourness better than pH. Chapters 0 and 1.	upstream chapter-0 term
titration	In a titration, a base of known concentration (here sodium hydroxide, NaOH) is added to a measured volume of brew until the pH reaches a chosen endpoint.	upstream chapter-0 term
total dissolved solids	Mass fraction of dissolved coffee solids in a brew, in percent. Chapter 2A.	upstream chapter-0 term
weak acid	Most acids in coffee are weak acids: at the pH of a brew, most of their molecules keep their hydrogen ions rather than releasing them.	upstream chapter-0 term

A calibration offset is identical in every reading and survives averaging.	upstream chapter-0 check

Why do researchers match roasts on both colour and mass loss?<br>(a) Colour readings are too imprecise to use<br>(b) Colour describes the ground surface, while mass loss reflects the whole bean, and the two can disagree<br>(c) Mass loss is required by the SCA standard	<b>(b) Colour describes the ground surface, while mass loss reflects the whole bean, and the two can disagree</b><br>Two roasts can match on one measure and differ on the other, especially when heating rates differ.	upstream chapter-0 check
affective test	Affective tests ask how much a person likes the result. A trained panel can agree that a coffee is intensely acidic and still disagree on whether the acidity is good, so the two questions should be kept apart.	upstream chapter-1 term

astringency	Nerves in the mouth detect temperature, thickness, particles and the drying, puckering sensation called astringency.	upstream chapter-1 term

chlorogenic acids	Esters of quinic acid with hydroxycinnamic acids; abundant in green coffee and precursors of bitter lactones and phenolic volatiles. Chapters 1, 6 and 8.	upstream chapter-1 term

detection threshold	The detection threshold is the lowest concentration at which a substance can be told apart from a blank.	upstream chapter-1 term
discrimination test	A discrimination test answers exactly that and nothing more.  | Test | Task | Probability of a correct guess | |---|---|---| | Triangle (ISO 4120) | Three cups, two alike: pick the odd one | 1/3 | | Duo-trio | A reference cup and two test cups: pick the test cup that matches the reference | 1/2 | | Two-alternative forced choice (2-AFC) | Two cups: pick the one with more of a named attribute | 1/2 | | Tetrad | Four cups, two of each sample: sort them into two pairs | 1/3 |	upstream chapter-1 term

gas chromatography	In gas chromatography (GC), a mixture of volatiles is carried by a gas through a long, thin column, and each compound leaves the column at its own characteristic time (Appendix D.6).	upstream chapter-1 term
gas chromatography-olfactometry	In gas chromatography-olfactometry (GC-O), the gas leaving the column is split: part goes to a detector, and part to a sniffing port where a trained assessor records each odour and when it appears.	upstream chapter-1 term
hierarchical clustering	Counting how often each pair of attributes was grouped together gave a measure of similarity, and hierarchical clustering, a method that repeatedly merges the most similar items into groups, produced a tree.	upstream chapter-1 term

mouthfeel	These sensations make up mouthfeel, which coffee tasters call body.  The brain combines the three inputs and refers them all to the mouth.	upstream chapter-1 term
null hypothesis	The analysis starts from a null hypothesis, the assumption that there is no perceptible difference, so that every taster is guessing with a probability of 1/3 of being right.	upstream chapter-1 term
odour activity value	Concentration of an odorant divided by its odour threshold. Chapter 1.	upstream chapter-1 term

olfactory receptor	Several hundred kinds of olfactory receptors in the upper nasal cavity respond to volatile compounds, substances that evaporate readily enough to travel through air.	upstream chapter-1 term
omission test	In an omission test, one compound at a time is left out of the mixture and tasters perform triangle tests to see whether its absence is noticed.	upstream chapter-1 term
orthonasal	Sniffing the cup carries them in through the nostrils (orthonasal smell). Drinking carries them from the back of the mouth up into the nasal cavity as you swallow and breathe out (retronasal smell).	upstream chapter-1 term
p-value	The p-value is the probability, computed under the null hypothesis, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed.	upstream chapter-1 term

recognition threshold	The recognition threshold, usually higher, is the concentration at which its quality can be named.	upstream chapter-1 term

brittle	Roasting dries the bean's cell walls and fills its cells with gas, turning a tough, moist seed into a brittle solid: one that breaks without first bending or stretching.	upstream chapter-4 term
comminution	Reducing a material to smaller particles is called comminution. Three classical laws relate the energy E per unit mass to the feed size d<sub>1</sub> and the product size d<sub>2</sub>.	upstream chapter-4 term
conical burrs	Conical burrs are a toothed cone turning inside a toothed ring; beans are drawn downward through a tapering gap.	upstream chapter-4 term
d50	The d50, or volume median, is the size below which half the volume lies; d<sub>10</sub> and d<sub>90</sub> are defined in the same way for 10% and 90%.	upstream chapter-4 term
fines	Particles below about 100 µm; a small share of mass, most of the particle count and much of the surface; they control bed permeability. Chapters 2B and 4.	upstream chapter-4 term
flat burrs	Flat burrs are two parallel toothed discs, one rotating. Beans enter at the centre, are broken progressively as they move outward, and leave at the rim once they fit through the gap.	upstream chapter-4 term
Griffith criterion	This Griffith criterion predicts that larger flaws need less force to grow. Large particles contain larger flaws and break easily; small particles contain only small flaws and resist.	upstream chapter-4 term
image analysis	Image analysis photographs particles spread on a contrasting surface and measures each one. A phone camera and free software resolve particles down to about 50 to 100 µm.	upstream chapter-4 term
laser diffraction	Laser diffraction disperses particles in air or liquid and shines a laser through them.	upstream chapter-4 term
number weighting	Number weighting counts every particle equally. - Volume weighting counts each particle in proportion to its volume, which scales as d<sup>3</sup>.	upstream chapter-4 term

fragmentation	In fragmentation, a molecule breaks into smaller pieces, as sugars do when heated.  ## 2.	upstream chapter-8 term

blocking	Blocking. When a nuisance factor cannot be held constant, arrange for each block of the experiment to contain every treatment.	upstream chapter-9 term
confidence interval	Report effect sizes with confidence intervals alongside p-values. A 95% confidence interval is a range constructed so that, over many repetitions of the experiment, 95% of such ranges would contain the true value.	upstream chapter-9 term
confounding	Many roasting comparisons are confounded: two variables change together, so their effects cannot be separated.	upstream chapter-9 term
control	Control. Hold every variable fixed except the one under study, and record what you cannot fix.	upstream chapter-9 term

interaction	It also estimates their interaction, which tells you whether the effect of one variable depends on the level of the other.	upstream chapter-9 term

randomisation	Randomisation. Decide the order of roasts, brews and servings by chance, so that slow drifts (a machine warming up, tasters tiring, room temperature changing) are not lined up with the treatment.	upstream chapter-9 term
replication	Replication. Repeat the treatment on independent experimental units, the things to which the treatment is applied.	upstream chapter-9 term

base	An acid is a substance that donates a hydrogen ion (a proton, H<sup>+</sup>); a base accepts one.	upstream appendix-A term
buffer capacity	Buffer capacity, the amount of strong acid or base needed to change the pH by one unit, is greatest when pH equals pK<sub>a</sub> and grows with the total concentration of the buffer.	upstream appendix-A term
chemical equilibrium	They reach a state of chemical equilibrium in which the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates, so concentrations stop changing.	upstream appendix-A term
conjugate base	The conjugate base of an acid HA is the species A<sup>−</sup> left after the proton is lost.	upstream appendix-A term

hydrate	The formula and molar mass of such a hydrate include that water. Epsom salt, MgSO<sub>4</sub>·7H<sub>2</sub>O, is 9.86% magnesium by mass (24.305/246.47), whereas anhydrous MgSO<sub>4</sub> is 20.2%.	upstream appendix-A term
ion product	If the product of the actual concentrations, the ion product, exceeds K<sub>sp</sub>, the solution is supersaturated and calcite can deposit as scale.	upstream appendix-A term
Le Chatelier's principle	Le Chatelier's principle summarises the consequence: a system at equilibrium responds to a change by partly reversing it.	upstream appendix-A term
mass concentration	Mass concentration is mass of solute per volume of solution, in g/L or mg/L.	upstream appendix-A term
mass fraction	Mass fraction is the mass of solute divided by the mass of solution. TDS is a mass fraction quoted in percent: a brew at 1.35% TDS has 1.35 g of dissolved solids per 100 g of brew.	upstream appendix-A term
molar mass	The molar mass M of a compound, in g/mol, is the sum of the masses of the atoms in its formula.	upstream appendix-A term
molarity	Molarity, in mol/L, counts particles per litre. It is the natural unit for reactions and equilibria, because reactions combine particles in fixed numbers.	upstream appendix-A term
mole	Chemists count particles in moles. One mole is 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> particles, a number chosen so that one mole of carbon-12 atoms weighs exactly 12 g.	upstream appendix-A term
parts per million	Parts per million (ppm) is a mass ratio: 1 ppm = 1 mg of solute per kg of solution.	upstream appendix-A term
polyprotic acid	Acids with more than one value are polyprotic: they can give up more than one proton, each with its own pK<sub>a</sub>.	upstream appendix-A term
reaction quotient	The reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but uses the concentrations present at any moment.	upstream appendix-A term
stoichiometry	A balanced chemical equation states the ratios in which particles react, and stoichiometry is the arithmetic that follows from those ratios.	upstream appendix-A term
supersaturated	If the product of the actual concentrations, the ion product, exceeds K<sub>sp</sub>, the solution is supersaturated and calcite can deposit as scale.	upstream appendix-A term
water of crystallisation	Some salts crystallise with water molecules built into their structure, called water of crystallisation.	upstream appendix-A term

aldol reaction	This aldol reaction is often followed by loss of water, giving a C=C double bond next to the C=O.	upstream appendix-B term
aromatic	A ring is aromatic when it is flat, every ring atom takes part in a continuous system of shared electrons, and that system contains 2, 6, 10 or, in general, 4n + 2 electrons (Hückel's rule).	upstream appendix-B term
benzene ring	A phenol has an OH group on a benzene ring, a flat six-carbon ring whose electrons are shared around the whole ring.	upstream appendix-B term
chiral	Stereoisomers differ in three-dimensional arrangement at a chiral carbon, one bonded to four different groups.	upstream appendix-B term
conjugate addition	The reaction adds the nucleophile to a carbon of the ring, a process called conjugate addition.	upstream appendix-B term
covalent bond	Carbon forms four covalent bonds, each a pair of electrons shared between two atoms.	upstream appendix-B term
disulfide	Two thiols oxidise to a disulfide, R–S–S–R:	upstream appendix-B term
double bond	Two atoms can share two pairs, a double bond, as in C=O and C=C.	upstream appendix-B term
electronegativity	Oxygen and nitrogen attract electrons more strongly than carbon and hydrogen do; this attraction is called electronegativity.	upstream appendix-B term
enol	The product, which has an OH on a double-bonded carbon, is an enol. A pair of forms like this, interconverting by moving a hydrogen and a double bond, are tautomers.	upstream appendix-B term
esterification	The reaction, esterification, is catalysed by acid and reversible:	upstream appendix-B term
hemiacetal	The OH on its fifth carbon attacks its own aldehyde, closing a six-membered ring called a hemiacetal.	upstream appendix-B term

isomer	Isomers are compounds with the same formula but different structures, and they can differ in taste, odour and reactivity.	upstream appendix-B term
nucleophilic addition	In nucleophilic addition, the nucleophile bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the pair of electrons from the C=O double bond moves onto the oxygen, which then picks up a proton.	upstream appendix-B term
ortho-quinone	A catechol, with two neighbouring OH groups, is oxidised by oxygen, especially when metal ions are present, to an ortho-quinone.	upstream appendix-B term
polar bond	When two atoms share electrons unequally, the bond is polar. Oxygen and nitrogen attract electrons more strongly than carbon and hydrogen do; this attraction is called electronegativity.	upstream appendix-B term
retro-aldol	The reverse reaction, retro-aldol fragmentation, splits a sugar between two carbons. It is how six-carbon sugars break into the two- and three-carbon fragments that become acetic acid, methylglyoxal and other small compounds during roasting.	upstream appendix-B term
tautomer	A pair of forms like this, interconverting by moving a hydrogen and a double bond, are tautomers.	upstream appendix-B term
thiol	A thiol, R–SH, is the sulfur counterpart of an alcohol. Sulfur is larger than oxygen and holds its outer electrons more loosely.	upstream appendix-B term
Why is the carbon of a C=O group attacked by nucleophiles?<br>(a) Oxygen draws electrons away, leaving the carbon partly positive<br>(b) The carbon carries a negative charge<br>(c) Carbon forms only two bonds	<b>(a) Oxygen draws electrons away, leaving the carbon partly positive</b><br>Oxygen is more electronegative, so the bond is polar and the carbon is electron-poor.	upstream appendix-B check

reaction order	The constant k is the rate constant, and n is the reaction order. The order is found by experiment; it cannot in general be read from the balanced equation.	upstream appendix-C term

chromatography	Chromatography separates a mixture by passing it through a column. A stationary phase is fixed inside the column and a mobile phase flows through it.	upstream appendix-D term
conductivity	Conductivity, in µS/cm, measures how well a solution carries electric current, which rises with the concentration and mobility of its ions.	upstream appendix-D term
constant mass	The usual test of completion is constant mass: successive weighings after further drying agree within a set tolerance.	upstream appendix-D term
electron ionisation	In electron ionisation, the standard source for GC-MS, energetic electrons knock an electron out of each molecule, and the resulting ion often breaks into fragments in a reproducible pattern that can be matched against libraries.	upstream appendix-D term
glass electrode	A glass electrode measures pH. A thin glass membrane develops an electrical potential that depends on the hydrogen-ion activity on each side.	upstream appendix-D term
gravimetry	Gravimetry measures mass. Oven drying gives moisture content (Chapter 6) and, applied to a brew, dissolved solids (Chapter 0).	upstream appendix-D term
high-performance liquid chromatography	High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) pumps a liquid mobile phase at high pressure through a packed column.	upstream appendix-D term
mass spectrometer	A mass spectrometer turns molecules into ions and separates the ions by their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z.	upstream appendix-D term
mobile phase	A stationary phase is fixed inside the column and a mobile phase flows through it.	upstream appendix-D term
nuclear magnetic resonance	Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy places a sample in a strong magnetic field and measures how atomic nuclei with magnetic properties, such as <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C, absorb radio-frequency energy.	upstream appendix-D term
primary standard	The titrant must be standardised, its exact concentration found by titrating a primary standard, a pure, stable substance weighed accurately.	upstream appendix-D term
retention time	Each compound spends a characteristic share of its time held by the stationary phase, so compounds leave the column at different retention times.	upstream appendix-D term

significance level	A small p-value, conventionally below the significance level α = 0.05, leads us to reject the null hypothesis.	upstream appendix-E term
t distribution	The t distribution is used instead of the normal distribution because s is itself an estimate; with few data, the interval must be wider to allow for that extra uncertainty.	upstream appendix-E term
t-test	A t-test asks whether a difference between two means is large compared with its standard error.	upstream appendix-E term
thurstonian model	Thurstonian models separate the two. They describe the sensory difference as d', the distance between the two samples' distributions of perceived intensity, measured in units of their standard deviation.	upstream appendix-E term
